Nbd7 develops the queen's knight and defends the knight on f6, so the pin does not cost the knight. This is the Cambridge Springs.
e3 supports the pawn on d4 and frees the light-squared bishop. The dark-squared bishop is already outside the chain.
c6 supports the pawn on d5 and leaves the queen a path toward the queenside.
Nf3 develops the king's knight. The queen is about to pin the other knight.
Qa5 attacks along the diagonal toward the knight on c3. The queen and the coming bishop are the idea.
Nd2 steps a knight onto the diagonal and defends the knight on c3. White unpins before the bishop arrives.
Bb4 develops the dark-squared bishop and attacks the knight on c3. The queen on a5 and this bishop are Black's active pieces.
Qc2 develops the queen and steps off the pin's file. She also watches the centre.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. Black castles with the queenside pressure already built.
Be2 develops the light-squared bishop and prepares castling. White finishes calmly against the pin.

qg9.intro: The Albin Counter-Gambit. Black plants a pawn on d4, and White fianchettos against it, castles, and trades the knights.
notes: d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
d5 meets White in the centre. Black is ready to decline or take the gambit pawn.
c4 attacks the pawn on d5. White offers a wing pawn: taking it draws the centre pawn off d5, and declining leaves the pressure on.
e5 offers a pawn to plant one on d4. This is the Albin, not a quiet decline.
dxe5 takes the pawn on e5 and accepts the gambit.
d4 plants the pawn in the centre. That wedge was the point of the offer.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on d4.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on d4.
g3 prepares a fianchetto against the pawn on d4. The long diagonal is how White handles the wedge.
Nge7 develops the king's knight toward g6, where it can help recover the pawn.
Bg2 puts the light-squared bishop on the long diagonal, eyeing the pawn on d4.
Ng6 eyes the pawn on e5. Black wants the gambit pawn back.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The king is safe behind the fianchetto.
Ngxe5 takes the pawn on e5. The gambit pawn comes back, and the knight on f3 can trade.
Nxe5 takes the knight on e5 and removes one defender of the pawn on d4.
Nxe5 recaptures the knight on e5. The knights come off, and the pawn on d4 remains the feature.
Na3 develops the queen's knight toward b5, where it can annoy the pawn on d4.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling.

qg10.intro: The Moscow. White takes the knight on f6, the queen recaptures, and Black prepares a fianchetto after taking on c4.
notes: d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
d5 meets White in the centre. Black is ready to decline or take the gambit pawn.
c4 attacks the pawn on d5. White offers a wing pawn: taking it draws the centre pawn off d5, and declining leaves the pressure on.
c6 supports the pawn on d5 and leaves the light-squared bishop free. That is the Slav.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and controls the centre before the queen's knight comes out.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and defends the centre.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d5.
e6 supports the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. The light-squared bishop stays in, which this line accepts.
Bg5 attacks the knight on f6 and offers the trade that defines the Moscow.
h6 asks the bishop on g5 a question before Black commits the king.
Bxf6 takes the knight on f6. White gives up the dark-squared bishop to spoil Black's development.
Qxf6 recaptures the bishop on f6. The queen comes out early, which is the price of the trade.
e3 supports the pawn on d4 and frees the light-squared bishop.
Nd7 develops the queen's knight and supports the centre. The king's knight has already been traded.
Bd3 develops the light-squared bishop and aims at the kingside.
dxc4 takes the pawn on c4. Black releases the centre now that the queen is out.
Bxc4 recaptures the pawn on c4. The bishop moves twice, and Black uses the tempo for a fianchetto.
g6 prepares the dark-squared bishop's fianchetto. The queen on f6 already sits beside that diagonal.

frb1.intro: The Winawer. The dark-squared bishop takes on c3, the queen comes to a5, and Black breaks with c4 and f6 before castling long.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e6 prepares a central pawn and shuts the light-squared bishop in. Black accepts that bishop for a solid centre.
d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
d5 challenges the pawn on e4 and builds the French centre. The light-squared bishop stays inside the chain.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d5. This is a main line, and the dark-squared bishop will pin the knight.
Bb4 pins the knight on c3 to the king on e1. The Winawer attacks that knight before the centre closes.
e5 gains space and shuts the knight's usual square. The centre is now a chain, and Black will hit its base.
c5 attacks the pawn on d4, the base of the chain. This is the French counterplay.
a3 asks the bishop on b4 whether it will take or retreat. Taking is the Winawer.
Bxc3+ takes the knight on c3 and gives check. White's pawn takes back, and the pawns are doubled.
bxc3 recaptures the bishop on c3. The pawns are doubled, which was the point of the trade.
Ne7 develops the king's knight toward the centre. The usual square is taken by White's pawn.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and defends the centre.
Bd7 develops the light-squared bishop and supports the queen coming out.
a4 gains space and slows Black's queenside. The queen comes out anyway.
Qa5 attacks the doubled pawns and develops the queen. She is the active piece in the Winawer.
Bd2 develops the dark-squared bishop and defends the pawn on c3 against the queen on a5.
Nbc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d4.
Bd3 develops the light-squared bishop and aims at the kingside.
c4 closes the queenside and fixes the doubled pawns. Black does not want the centre opened while the king is still uncastled.
Be2 drops the light-squared bishop back. The pawn on c4 has taken its old diagonal.
f6 challenges the pawn on e5 and starts the central break. The king will castle the other way.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. White castles into the side Black is breaking.
O-O-O brings the king to c8 and the rook to d8. Black castles long, away from the f-file break.

frb2.intro: Advance French with the queen on b6. The knight comes via h6 to f5, and the e-pawn takes the bishop.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e6 prepares a central pawn and shuts the light-squared bishop in. Black accepts that bishop for a solid centre.
d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
d5 challenges the pawn on e4 and builds the French centre. The light-squared bishop stays inside the chain.
e5 gains space and clamps the centre. The Advance chain is the thing Black must attack.
c5 attacks the pawn on d4, the base of the chain.
c3 supports the pawn on d4 and keeps the chain intact.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d4.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and defends the pawn on d4.
Qb6 attacks the pawn on d4 again and eyes the pawn on b2. The queen is the Advance idea in this line.
Be2 develops the light-squared bishop and prepares castling. It does not block the defence of d4.
cxd4 takes the pawn on d4 and opens the c-file.
cxd4 recaptures the pawn on d4 and keeps a pawn in the centre. The c-file is open.
Nh6 develops the king's knight toward f5. The usual square is taken by the pawn on e5.
Bd3 develops the light-squared bishop and aims at the knight's coming square.
Bd7 develops the light-squared bishop and connects the queen with the other pieces.
Bc2 drops the light-squared bishop back, keeping it on the diagonal toward the kingside.
Nf5 plants the knight on the square that attacks the pawn on d4. The bishop on c2 is aimed at this knight.
Bxf5 takes the knight on f5. White removes the piece that was pressing d4.
exf5 recaptures the bishop on f5. The e-pawn takes, so the light-squared bishop's diagonal opens a little.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1.
Be6 develops the light-squared bishop to a solid square and completes the minor pieces.

frb3.intro: Advance French with the bishop on d7. The knight goes to g6, steps to h8 when the h-pawn arrives, and Black breaks with f6.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e6 prepares a central pawn and shuts the light-squared bishop in. Black accepts that bishop for a solid centre.
d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
d5 challenges the pawn on e4 and builds the French centre. The light-squared bishop stays inside the chain.
e5 gains space and clamps the centre. The Advance chain is the thing Black must attack.
c5 attacks the pawn on d4, the base of the chain.
c3 supports the pawn on d4 and keeps the chain intact.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d4.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and defends the pawn on d4.
Bd7 develops the light-squared bishop and leaves the queen at home. This is the quieter Advance.
Be2 develops the light-squared bishop and prepares castling.
Nge7 develops the king's knight toward g6. The pawn on e5 has taken the usual square.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1.
Ng6 brings the knight to the kingside, where it eyes the centre and the castled king.
g3 gives the king a flight and prepares to push the h-pawn. The knight on g6 is the target.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling.
h4 starts the pawn rush against the knight on g6.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. Black castles before the h-pawn arrives.
h5 kicks the knight on g6. The retreat is backward, which this line accepts.
Nh8 steps the knight home, off the pawn on h5. It is passive, and the centre break will matter more.
Bf4 develops the dark-squared bishop and holds the chain.
cxd4 takes the pawn on d4 and opens the c-file. Black times the capture after castling.
cxd4 recaptures the pawn on d4 and keeps the central pawn.
Be8 tucks the light-squared bishop back so the f-pawn can move, and it can redeploy.
Kg2 steps the king up and connects the rooks. White is shuffling while Black prepares the break.
f6 challenges the pawn on e5. This is the French break against the chain.
Rh1 puts the rook back on the h-file. It does not answer the break.
fxe5 takes the pawn on e5 and opens the f-file. The chain has been challenged.

frb4.intro: The open Tarrasch. Both sides recapture with pawns, Black accepts an isolated pawn, and the light-squared bishop comes to g4.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e6 prepares a central pawn and shuts the light-squared bishop in. Black accepts that bishop for a solid centre.
d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
d5 challenges the pawn on e4 and builds the French centre. The light-squared bishop stays inside the chain.
Nd2 is the Tarrasch. The queen's knight develops without blocking the c-pawn, and it defends the pawn on e4.
c5 attacks the pawn on d4 and strikes before the centre closes.
exd5 takes the pawn on d5 and opens the centre. This is the open Tarrasch.
exd5 recaptures the pawn on d5. Black accepts an isolated pawn for open lines and piece play.
Ngf3 develops the king's knight and prepares castling.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on d5.
Bb5 pins the knight on c6 to the king, now that the d-pawn has left home, and develops the light-squared bishop.
Bd6 develops the dark-squared bishop onto an active square and prepares castling.
dxc5 takes the pawn on c5 and removes one of Black's central pawns.
Bxc5 recaptures the pawn on c5. The dark-squared bishop stays active.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1.
Ne7 develops the king's knight and can reinforce the centre or move the other knight.
Nb3 attacks the bishop on c5 and improves the queen's knight.
Bd6 drops the dark-squared bishop back and keeps it. The bishop still aims at the kingside.
Re1 puts the rook on the open e-file.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8.
Bg5 develops the dark-squared bishop and asks the knight on e7 a question.
Bg4 develops the light-squared bishop and gets ready to pin the knight on f3. The isolated pawn is the long-term feature of the position.

frb5.intro: The closed Tarrasch. The knight drops to d7, Black breaks with f6, and the knight lands on e4 after the bishops trade.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e6 prepares a central pawn and shuts the light-squared bishop in. Black accepts that bishop for a solid centre.
d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
d5 challenges the pawn on e4 and builds the French centre. The light-squared bishop stays inside the chain.
Nd2 is the Tarrasch. The queen's knight develops without blocking the c-pawn, and it defends the pawn on e4.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4. White will kick it.
e5 kicks the king's knight and gains space. The centre closes.
Nfd7 drops the knight back and keeps it flexible. From d7 it supports the c-pawn break.
Bd3 develops the light-squared bishop and aims at the kingside.
c5 attacks the pawn on d4, the base of the chain.
c3 supports the pawn on d4.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d4.
Ne2 develops the king's knight without blocking the f-pawn. White keeps f4 in reserve.
cxd4 takes the pawn on d4 and opens the c-file.
cxd4 recaptures the pawn on d4 and keeps the central pawn.
f6 challenges the pawn on e5. The closed centre has to be broken.
exf6 takes the pawn on f6 and opens the position.
Nxf6 recaptures the pawn on f6. The knight returns to a natural square.
Nf3 brings the knight from e2 to its natural square now that the king's knight has moved.
Bd6 develops the dark-squared bishop onto an active diagonal.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8.
Bf4 offers a trade of dark-squared bishops and challenges the bishop on d6.
Bxf4 takes the bishop on f4. Black is happy to trade this bishop once it has done its job.
Nxf4 recaptures the bishop on f4. The knight lands on an active square.
Ne4 plants the knight on the central outpost. That was the point of the break and the trades.

frb6.intro: The Classical French. Be7 meets the pin, the queen takes on e7, and the light-squared bishop comes to b7.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e6 prepares a central pawn and shuts the light-squared bishop in. Black accepts that bishop for a solid centre.
d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
d5 challenges the pawn on e4 and builds the French centre. The light-squared bishop stays inside the chain.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d5.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
Bg5 pins the knight on f6 to the queen on d8. Black should break the pin before the centre closes.
Be7 steps the dark-squared bishop between the knight and the queen and breaks the pin.
e5 kicks the knight and gains space. The pin is gone, so the knight can drop back.
Nfd7 drops the knight back and keeps the dark-squared bishop's trade available.
Bxe7 takes the bishop on e7. White removes the bishop that broke the pin.
Qxe7 recaptures the bishop on e7. The queen comes out, which this line wants.
f4 supports the pawn on e5 and gains kingside space.
a6 gains a little space and prepares the queenside pawn push.
Nf3 develops the king's knight.
c5 attacks the pawn on d4, the base of the chain.
Qd2 develops the queen and connects the rooks once White castles.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d4.
dxc5 takes the pawn on c5 and opens lines.
Nxc5 recaptures the pawn on c5. The knight from d7 arrives on an active square.
Bd3 develops the light-squared bishop and aims at the kingside.
b5 gains queenside space and prepares the light-squared bishop.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1.
Bb7 develops the light-squared bishop on the long diagonal. The French bishop finally has a square.

frb7.intro: The Steinitz French. The knight drops to d7, the c-pawn hits d4, and the queen comes to b6.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e6 prepares a central pawn and shuts the light-squared bishop in. Black accepts that bishop for a solid centre.
d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
d5 challenges the pawn on e4 and builds the French centre. The light-squared bishop stays inside the chain.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d5.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
e5 kicks the knight on f6 and gains space.
Nfd7 drops the knight back. The Steinitz keeps the knight flexible and supports the c-pawn.
f4 supports the pawn on e5 and builds a big pawn centre.
c5 attacks the pawn on d4, the base of that centre.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and defends the pawn on d4.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d4.
Be3 develops the dark-squared bishop and defends the pawn on d4.
Qb6 attacks the pawn on d4 and the pawn on b2. The queen adds a third attacker to the base.
a3 stops the dark-squared bishop landing on b4 and prepares queenside space.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling. The pressure on d4 is already built.

frb8.intro: The Exchange French. The centre opens, Black pins the knight, and the bishop drops to f5 to be traded before castling.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e6 prepares a central pawn and shuts the light-squared bishop in. Black accepts that bishop for a solid centre.
d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
d5 challenges the pawn on e4 and builds the French centre. The light-squared bishop stays inside the chain.
exd5 takes the pawn on d5 and offers an open centre. The French tension is released at once.
exd5 recaptures the pawn on d5 and opens the e-file. Black has a pawn in the centre and a free light-squared bishop.
Bd3 develops the light-squared bishop onto an active diagonal.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d4.
c3 supports the pawn on d4 and blunts the knight on c6.
Bd6 develops the dark-squared bishop and aims at the kingside.
Nf3 develops the king's knight. It can be pinned.
Nge7 develops the king's knight and leaves the light-squared bishop a free path.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1.
Bg4 pins the knight on f3 to the queen on d1. The pin is the active idea in this open centre.
h3 asks the bishop on g4 a question.
Bf5 keeps the light-squared bishop and offers the trade on f5 rather than giving it up for the knight.
Bxf5 takes the bishop on f5. White accepts the trade of light-squared bishops.
Nxf5 recaptures the bishop on f5. The knight from e7 arrives on an active square.
Re1+ puts the rook on the open e-file and gives check. The knight will step back in front of the king.
Nfe7 drops the knight back and blocks the check. The king is no longer in check, and the knight covers the file.
a4 gains queenside space before Black castles.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. The king steps off the e-file.

frb9.intro: The Rubinstein. Black takes on e4, the knights trade on f6, and the queen comes to a5 with check.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e6 prepares a central pawn and shuts the light-squared bishop in. Black accepts that bishop for a solid centre.
d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
d5 challenges the pawn on e4 and builds the French centre. The light-squared bishop stays inside the chain.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d5.
dxe4 takes the pawn on e4 and releases the centre. The Rubinstein simplifies rather than keeping the chain.
Nxe4 recaptures the pawn on e4. The knight stands in the centre.
Nd7 develops the queen's knight and prepares to challenge that central knight.
Nf3 develops the king's knight.
Ngf6 attacks the knight on e4. Black offers the trade.
Nxf6+ takes the knight on f6 and gives check. Black chooses the knight recapture.
Nxf6 recaptures the knight on f6 and gets out of check. The knights come off.
Bd3 develops the light-squared bishop and aims at the kingside.
c5 attacks the pawn on d4 and fights for the centre.
dxc5 takes the pawn on c5 and opens the position.
Bxc5 recaptures the pawn on c5. The dark-squared bishop comes to an active diagonal, and Black can castle.
Qe2 develops the queen onto the e-file.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8.
Bg5 attacks the knight on f6 and offers a pin.
h6 asks the bishop on g5 a question before it settles.
Bh4 keeps the dark-squared bishop and maintains the pressure on the knight.
Qa5+ develops the queen with check. She steps onto the fifth rank while White's king is still in the centre.

frb10.intro: The King's Indian Attack against the French. Black castles, expands on the queenside, then drives the dark-squared bishop back and breaks with the knight and the f-pawn.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e6 prepares a central pawn and shuts the light-squared bishop in. Black accepts that bishop for a solid centre.
d3 is a quiet centre. White is not playing the classical pawn duo, and the king's bishop will fianchetto.
d5 challenges the pawn on e4. Black takes a French centre even against this setup.
Nd2 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e4. The c-pawn stays free.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
Ngf3 develops the king's knight.
c5 gains space and stakes a claim on the queenside. The d-pawn is already in the centre.
g3 prepares the fianchetto. This is the King's Indian Attack.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and supports the centre.
Bg2 puts the light-squared bishop on the long diagonal.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. Both kings are safe, and Black can expand.
Re1 puts the rook behind the pawn on e4, ready for a central push.
b5 gains queenside space. The pawns will roll before White's centre moves.
e5 gains space and kicks the knight on f6.
Nd7 drops the knight back and supports a later break.
Nf1 reroutes the queen's knight toward the kingside. The centre pawn has done its job of gaining space.
a5 continues the queenside advance.
Bf4 develops the dark-squared bishop to an active square.
g5 asks that bishop a question and gains kingside space. The king is already castled, so this push is a plan, not a looseness.
Be3 drops the dark-squared bishop back and keeps it. The pawn on g5 has done its job.
g4 pushes on and cramps the knight on f3.
N3d2 drops the king's knight back, off the pawn.
Ncxe5 takes the pawn on e5. The knight from c6 collects the advanced pawn.
Nb3 improves the queen's knight and eyes the queenside.
f5 challenges the centre and opens lines for the rooks. The kingside pawns and this break are the counterplay.

rlw1.intro: The Breyer Ruy. The bishop retreats to a4, the knight reroutes via b8 to d7, and White finishes with the knight to f1.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bb5 attacks the knight on c6. The pawn on d7 still stands between that knight and the king, so this is pressure, not yet a full pin.
a6 asks the light-squared bishop a question. Black wants to know if White will trade or keep it.
Ba4 keeps the light-squared bishop. Retreating rather than taking keeps that bishop for later, and the pawn on d7 still stops a full pin.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The king is safe before the centre opens.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling. It also defends the knight on f6.
Re1 puts the rook behind the pawn on e4, so that pawn is defended.
b5 attacks the bishop on a4 and gains queenside space.
Bb3 keeps the light-squared bishop and steps off the pawn. The diagonal toward f7 stays open.
d6 supports the pawn on e5 and frees the light-squared bishop. The centre stays closed.
c3 prepares a central pawn and gives the bishop a square to drop to.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8.
h3 stops a piece landing on g4 and gives the king air before the centre opens.
Nb8 starts the Breyer reroute. The knight leaves c6 so the c-pawn can move, and it is heading for d7.
d4 opens the centre at last. The preparation is done.
Nbd7 completes the reroute and supports the pawn on e5.
Nbd2 develops the queen's knight toward the kingside. The Spanish knight manoeuvre has started.
Bb7 puts the light-squared bishop on the long diagonal.
Bc2 tucks the light-squared bishop back, ready for the kingside once the centre opens.
Re8 puts the rook on the e-file, behind the pawn on e5.
Nf1 continues the knight manoeuvre toward the kingside. From here the knight can go to g3.

rlw2.intro: The Arkhangelsk. Black fianchettos early, and White meets it with a quiet centre, a4, and the bishop on a2.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bb5 attacks the knight on c6. The pawn on d7 still stands between that knight and the king, so this is pressure, not yet a full pin.
a6 asks the light-squared bishop a question. Black wants to know if White will trade or keep it.
Ba4 keeps the light-squared bishop. Retreating rather than taking keeps that bishop for later, and the pawn on d7 still stops a full pin.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1.
b5 attacks the light-squared bishop and gains space before the dark-squared bishop comes out.
Bb3 keeps the light-squared bishop and aims toward f7.
Bb7 puts the light-squared bishop on the long diagonal. This early fianchetto is the Arkhangelsk.
d3 supports the pawn on e4 and frees the dark-squared bishop. White stays solid against the fianchetto.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling.
a4 attacks the pawn on b5 and challenges the queenside expansion.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8.
Re1 puts the rook behind the pawn on e4.
d6 supports the pawn on e5 and keeps the centre closed.
Nbd2 develops the queen's knight and supports the centre.
Na5 attacks the bishop on b3. Black wants that bishop off its diagonal.
Ba2 keeps the light-squared bishop and steps off the knight. The diagonal toward f7 remains.

rlw3.intro: The Berlin. Queens come off, the black king steps to d8 and back, and White builds with the rook and the knight on e4.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bb5 attacks the knight on c6. The pawn on d7 still stands between that knight and the king, so this is pressure, not yet a full pin.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4. Black does not ask the bishop a question first, so this is the Berlin.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The pawn on e4 is offered.
Nxe4 takes the pawn on e4. Black accepts the pawn, and the centre will open.
d4 attacks the pawn on e5 and opens lines while the king is already castled.
Nd6 attacks the bishop on b5 and drops the knight back into the centre.
Bxc6 takes the knight on c6. White damages the queenside pawns rather than save the bishop.
dxc6 recaptures the bishop on c6 and opens the d-file. The pawns are doubled.
dxe5 takes the pawn on e5 and opens the centre. The knight on d6 is asked to move.
Nf5 steps the knight off the pawn and toward an active square.
Qxd8+ takes the queen on d8 and gives check. The Berlin endgame starts here.
Kxd8 takes the queen on d8 and gets out of check. The king is in the centre, which this line accepts.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and eyes the centre.
Ke8 steps the king back toward safety. It is not castling, but it leaves the d-file.
h3 gives the king air and takes g4 away from Black's pieces.
Be6 develops the light-squared bishop to a solid square.
Rd1 puts the rook on the open d-file. The king has stepped aside to e8.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and covers the king.
Ne4 plants the knight in the centre. The endgame play is about this knight and the open file.

rlw4.intro: The Open Defence. Black takes on e4, holds the centre with d5, and White builds with c3, the knight on d2, and the bishop on c2.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bb5 attacks the knight on c6. The pawn on d7 still stands between that knight and the king, so this is pressure, not yet a full pin.
a6 asks the light-squared bishop a question.
Ba4 keeps the light-squared bishop. Retreating rather than taking keeps that bishop for later.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The pawn on e4 can be taken.
Nxe4 takes the pawn on e4. This capture is the Open Defence.
d4 challenges the pawn on e5 and opens lines. White does not take the knight back at once.
b5 attacks the bishop on a4 and gains space.
Bb3 keeps the light-squared bishop on the diagonal toward the centre.
d5 plants a pawn in the centre and blunts the bishop on b3. The Open Defence is built on this pawn.
dxe5 takes the pawn on e5 and opens the centre. The knight on e4 stays for the moment.
Be6 develops the light-squared bishop and challenges the bishop on b3.
c3 supports the centre and gives the light-squared bishop a retreat.
Bc5 develops the dark-squared bishop onto an active diagonal.
Nbd2 develops the queen's knight and challenges the knight on e4.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8.
Bc2 steps the light-squared bishop off the bishop on e6 and keeps it.
Nxd2 takes the knight on d2. Black removes the piece that was challenging the centre.
Qxd2 recaptures the knight on d2 and develops the queen.

rlw5.intro: The Exchange Ruy. White takes on c6, queens come off, and the knight lands on c4 against the bishop on d6.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bb5 attacks the knight on c6. The pawn on d7 still stands between that knight and the king, so this is pressure, not yet a full pin.
a6 asks the bishop on b5 a question. In this line White takes.
Bxc6 takes the knight on c6. White gives up the bishop pair to damage Black's pawns.
dxc6 recaptures the bishop on c6 and opens the d-file. The pawns are doubled.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1.
f6 supports the pawn on e5. The king's side is a little airy, which this structure accepts.
d4 opens the centre and attacks the pawn on e5.
Bg4 pins the knight on f3 to the queen on d1. The pin is real.
dxe5 takes the pawn on e5 and opens the d-file. The queens now face each other.
Qxd1 takes the queen on d1. Black is happy to trade into the endgame.
Rxd1 recaptures the queen on d1. The rook arrives on the open file.
fxe5 takes the pawn on e5 and restores a pawn in the centre.
Rd3 lifts the rook. It can swing along the third rank and keep pressure.
Bd6 develops the dark-squared bishop and defends the pawn on e5.
Nbd2 develops the queen's knight toward c4.
Nf6 develops the king's knight.
Nc4 attacks the bishop on d6 and the pawn on e5. That is the square the knight was heading for.

rlw6.intro: The Schliemann. Black strikes with the f-pawn, White's knights take in the centre, and the g-pawn recaptures before both sides castle.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bb5 attacks the knight on c6. The pawn on d7 still stands between that knight and the king, so this is pressure, not yet a full pin.
f5 is the Schliemann. Black challenges the pawn on e4 at once and accepts an open king's side.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e4. White meets the gambit with a piece.
fxe4 takes the pawn on e4 and opens the f-file.
Nxe4 recaptures the pawn on e4. The knight stands in the centre.
Nf6 attacks the knight on e4 and develops the king's knight.
Qe2 develops the queen and defends the knight on e4. She also eyes the e-file.
d5 attacks the knight on e4 and claims the centre.
Nxf6+ takes the knight on f6 and gives check.
gxf6 recaptures the knight on f6 and gets out of check. The king's side pawns are doubled.
d4 opens the centre against the pawn on e5.
Bg7 puts the dark-squared bishop on the long diagonal and prepares castling.
dxe5 takes the pawn on e5 and opens lines.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. Black castles despite the doubled pawns.
Bxc6 takes the knight on c6 and damages the queenside as well.
bxc6 recaptures the bishop on c6. More doubled pawns, and the bishop on g7 stays.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. White castles once the tactics have settled.

rlw7.intro: The Classical Ruy with the bishop on c5. White opens the centre, the queen comes to d5, and then steps home once the knight has moved.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bb5 attacks the knight on c6. The pawn on d7 still stands between that knight and the king, so this is pressure, not yet a full pin.
Bc5 develops the dark-squared bishop and aims at the pawn on f2. This is the Classical, not the closed Ruy.
c3 prepares the central pawn push and takes b4 away from the bishop.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8.
d4 attacks the bishop on c5 and opens the centre.
Bb6 keeps the dark-squared bishop and steps off the pawn.
dxe5 takes the pawn on e5 and opens the centre. The new pawn attacks the knight on f6.
Nxe4 takes the pawn on e4. The knight jumps into the centre.
Qd5 attacks the undefended knight on e4. She also hits the knight on c6.
Nc5 steps the knight off the queen.
Bg5 develops the dark-squared bishop and attacks the queen on d8.
Ne7 steps the queen's knight in front of the queen and attacks the queen on d5.
Qd1 steps the queen off that knight and back home.

rlw8.intro: The Old Steinitz. Black plays d6, the centre opens, and White drops the bishop back to f1 before bringing the knight to f3.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bb5 attacks the knight on c6. The pawn on d7 still stands between that knight and the king, so this is pressure, not yet a full pin.
d6 supports the pawn on e5 and keeps the position solid. This is the Old Steinitz, a little cramped.
d4 opens the centre at once. Against this passive pawn, White does not wait.
Bd7 develops the light-squared bishop and breaks the pressure on the knight on c6.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and supports the centre.
Nf6 develops the king's knight.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling.
Re1 puts the rook on the e-file.
exd4 takes the pawn on d4 and releases the centre.
Nxd4 recaptures the pawn on d4 and puts a knight in the centre.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8.
Bf1 brings the light-squared bishop home. White keeps it rather than trade it on c6.
Re8 puts the rook on the e-file.
Nf3 brings the knight back from d4, and the queen on d1 looks up the file at the pawn on d6.

rlw9.intro: The Bird Defence. The knight jumps to d4, White takes and castles, and the bishop comes to c4 before the centre is settled with d3.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bb5 attacks the queen's knight. The pawn in front of the king still stands between that knight and the king, so this is pressure, not yet a full pin.
Nd4 is the Bird jump. The knight attacks the bishop on b5 and offers itself to be taken.
Nxd4 takes the knight on d4. White removes the jumper rather than moving the bishop.
exd4 recaptures the knight on d4. Black has a pawn in the centre.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The king leaves before that pawn becomes a problem.
c6 attacks the bishop on b5 and supports the pawn on d4.
Bc4 steps the light-squared bishop off the pawn and aims at the pawn on f7.
Nf6 develops the king's knight.
Re1 puts the rook on the half-open e-file.
d6 supports the pawn on d4 and frees the light-squared bishop.
c3 attacks the pawn on d4 and challenges the wedge.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling.
cxd4 takes the pawn on d4 and removes the wedge.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8.
d3 supports the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. The position has settled into a normal open game.

rlw10.intro: The Marshall Gambit. Black gives a pawn for an attack, the queen comes to h4 and h3, and White meets it with g3, the bishop, and the queen.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bb5 attacks the queen's knight. The pawn in front of the king still stands between that knight and the king, so this is pressure, not yet a full pin.
a6 asks the light-squared bishop a question.
Ba4 keeps the light-squared bishop. Retreating rather than taking keeps that bishop for later.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling.
Re1 puts the rook behind the pawn on e4.
b5 attacks the bishop on a4 and gains space.
Bb3 keeps the light-squared bishop and aims toward f7.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. Black castles before the gambit.
c3 prepares the central pawn. In the Marshall, Black strikes before that pawn arrives.
d5 offers a pawn to open lines against the castled king. This is the Marshall Gambit.
exd5 takes the pawn on d5 and accepts the gambit.
Nxd5 recaptures the pawn on d5 and plants the knight in the centre.
Nxe5 takes the pawn on e5. White collects the gambit pawn.
Nxe5 takes the knight on e5. The knights come off.
Rxe5 recaptures the knight on e5. The rook steps into the centre, which the attack will chase.
c6 attacks the knight on d5 and supports the centre. The attack needs this pawn move.
d4 supports the centre and opens a path for the dark-squared bishop.
Bd6 develops the dark-squared bishop and attacks the rook on e5. The rook should leave.
Re1 steps the rook off the bishop and back to the e-file.
Qh4 brings the queen out toward the king on g1. The attack has started.
g3 asks the queen a question and gives the king air. The pawn also blunts the bishop on d6.
Qh3 steps the queen off the pawn and attacks the pawn on h2.
Be3 develops the dark-squared bishop and covers the kingside.
Bg4 develops the light-squared bishop and attacks the queen on d1.
Qd3 steps the queen off the bishop and helps the defence.
Rae8 puts the other rook on the e-file. Both black rooks are now in the attack.
Nbd2 develops the queen's knight and finishes the book defence against the Marshall.

sib1.intro: The Najdorf, English Attack. Black kicks the knight with e5, both sides castle on opposite wings, and the pawn storms start with g4 and b5.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
c5 fights for the centre from the flank. This is the Sicilian.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and prepares to open the centre.
d6 keeps the centre compact and lets the king's knight come out. This is a Najdorf.
d4 opens the centre and offers a pawn to put a knight on the central square.
cxd4 takes the pawn on d4 and opens the c-file. That file is Black's main highway.
Nxd4 recaptures the pawn on d4. The knight sits in the centre.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e4.
a6 is the Najdorf move. It keeps a white knight off the square in front of Black's queenside and prepares expansion there.
Be3 develops the dark-squared bishop. White is building toward castling on the queenside.
e5 attacks the knight on d4 and gains space. The pawn on d6 stays back, which this line accepts.
Nb3 steps the knight off the pawn and leaves the dark-squared bishop on e3.
Be6 develops the light-squared bishop to an active square before the centre closes up.
f3 supports the pawn on e4 and prepares a kingside pawn advance.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling.
Qd2 develops the queen beside the bishop on e3 and prepares queenside castling.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8.
O-O-O brings the king to c1 and the rook to d1. The kings are now on opposite sides.
Nbd7 develops the queen's knight without blocking the c-file.
g4 starts the pawn storm against the castled king.
b5 starts Black's own pawn storm on the queenside.

sib2.intro: The Dragon. The bishop fianchettoes, both sides castle long and short, and Black breaks with d5 before the queens settle on the b-file.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
c5 fights for the centre from the flank. This is the Sicilian.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and prepares to open the centre.
d6 controls e5 and lets the king's knight come out.
d4 opens the centre and offers a pawn to put a knight on the central square.
cxd4 takes the pawn on d4 and opens the c-file.
Nxd4 recaptures the pawn on d4. The knight sits in the centre.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e4.
g6 prepares the fianchetto. The Dragon bishop belongs on the long diagonal.
Be3 develops the dark-squared bishop and eyes that long diagonal.
Bg7 puts the dark-squared bishop on the long diagonal. This is the Dragon.
f3 supports the pawn on e4 and prepares a kingside advance. It also takes the pin square away from the knight on f6.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. The king sits behind the fianchetto.
Qd2 develops the queen beside the bishop on e3. White is ready to castle long.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the knight on d4.
O-O-O brings the king to c1 and the rook to d1. Opposite-side castling means both attacks will race.
d5 breaks in the centre and attacks the pawn on e4. The Dragon wants this strike before White's attack lands.
exd5 takes the pawn on d5 and accepts the opening of the centre.
Nxd5 recaptures the pawn on d5. The knight arrives in the centre.
Nxc6 takes the knight on c6 and damages the queenside pawns.
bxc6 recaptures the knight on c6. The b-file opens against White's queenside.
Bd4 offers a trade of the dark-squared bishops. White wants the Dragon bishop off the long diagonal.
Bxd4 takes the bishop on d4. Black accepts the trade.
Qxd4 recaptures the bishop on d4. The queen stands in the centre.
Qb6 attacks the queen on d4 and puts pressure down the open b-file.
Na4 attacks the queen on b6 and steps the knight toward the queenside.
Qa5 steps the queen off the knight and keeps her on the queenside.

sib3.intro: The Richter-Rauzer. The bishop pins from g5, White castles long and plays f4, and the queens meet on the d-file.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
c5 fights for the centre from the flank. This is the Sicilian.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and prepares to open the centre.
d6 controls e5 and lets the king's knight come out.
d4 opens the centre and offers a pawn to put a knight on the central square.
cxd4 takes the pawn on d4 and opens the c-file.

Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e4.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the knight on d4.
Bg5 pins the knight on f6 to the queen on d8. This pin is the Rauzer.

Qd2 develops the queen and prepares queenside castling. She also stands behind the bishop on g5.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and breaks the pin on the knight on f6.
O-O-O brings the king to c1 and the rook to d1. The rook looks up the half-open d-file.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8.

Qxd4 recaptures the knight on d4. The queen takes a central post.
Qa5 attacks the knight on c3 and develops the queen.
Kb1 steps the king off the c-file. Black's c-file is already half open.
Rd8 puts the rook on the d-file, behind the pawn on d6.

sib4.intro: The Sveshnikov. Black plays e5, the knight hops via b5 to a3, and the other knight lands on d5 before the dark-squared bishops meet again.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
c5 fights for the centre from the flank. This is the Sicilian.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and prepares to open the centre.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and fights for the central squares.
d4 opens the centre and offers a pawn to put a knight on the central square.

Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e4.
e5 attacks the knight on d4 and gains space. Black accepts a hole in the centre for that space.
Ndb5 jumps deep into Black's position. That knight has to be met.

Bg5 pins the knight on f6 to the queen on d8.
a6 asks the knight a question and begins the queenside advance.
Na3 steps the knight to the edge. The other knight is the one headed for the central hole.

Nd5 plants the queen's knight on the hole. This is the square the Sveshnikov is built around.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and breaks the pin on the knight on f6.
Bxf6 takes the knight on f6. White removes a defender of the dark squares.
Bxf6 recaptures the bishop on f6. The dark-squared bishop takes up an active post.

Bg5 offers a trade of the dark-squared bishops and asks the bishop on f6 a question.

sib5.intro: A sharp open Sicilian with e6. White pushes e5, the queen comes to b6 with check, and the king steps to e2 before Black hits the knight with the f-pawn.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
c5 fights for the centre from the flank. This is the Sicilian.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and prepares to open the centre.
e6 supports a central pawn and frees the dark-squared bishop. Black keeps the position flexible.
d4 opens the centre and offers a pawn to put a knight on the central square.
cxd4 takes the pawn on d4 and opens the c-file.
Nxd4 recaptures the pawn on d4. The knight sits in the centre.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e4.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the knight on d4.

sib6.intro: The Alapin. White plays c3 and meets d5, the queen recaptures, and a knight jump to b5 sends her home.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.

Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the queen on d5.

O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and attacks the queen on d5.
Qd6 steps the queen off the knight and stays active.
Nb5 attacks the queen on d6. The early queen is chased again.

sib7.intro: The Smith-Morra Gambit. White offers a pawn for development, the bishop comes to c4, and the rook lands on the half-open d-file.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.

Bf4 develops the dark-squared bishop and eyes the queen on c7.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling.

sib8.intro: The Grand Prix Attack. White plays f4 and Bb5, Black trades that bishop, and the centre opens with d5 and d4.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.

Nf6 develops the king's knight.

Nxd5 takes the pawn on d5 and plants the knight in the centre.

sib9.intro: The Rossolimo. The bishop takes on c6, Black recaptures toward the centre, and both sides fix the queenside with a4 and a5.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
c5 fights for the centre from the flank. This is the Sicilian.

notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
